paper_title: RealCompanion: Benchmarking Human Understanding from Reasoning over Longitudinal Real-World Conversations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: An AI companion that talks with someone for months should come to understand them. It should know who they are, remember what they said, and recognize when something from the past matters now. Testing this needs real conversations, but real conversations are private, so existing benchmarks use invented people and invented questions. We release RealCompanion, ten real relationships between people and an AI companion, with 27,218 messages over up to 120 days. For each person, we release the full conversation, a profile, a persona, chat test items, and question test items. Every label points to the messages that support it, and every chat label comes with the reasoning that produced it. The real data shows three things. First, people rarely refer back. Only 3.4% of their messages depend on something said earlier, and when one does, the earlier message is usually far away (a median of 2,157 messages back). Averages hide this. Looking at the most recent messages finds the needed one 95.9% of the time overall, but only 2.2% of the time when it is far back. Second, AI systems cannot tell when the past matters. The detectors we tested barely beat chance on real messages, and when the same earlier messages are labeled "memories" instead of "earlier messages", models bring up the past 10 to 14 percentage points more often, even when nothing from the past is needed. Third, AI systems read more into a person than the person revealed. Three agent systems rebuild each persona equally well (F1 0.71). They see the person, and then imagine more. Understanding a person depends on knowing when their past matters and where what they shared ends, and only real conversations can test it.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: People now spend long time talking to AI companions. Understanding such person means answering two questions. The first is who they are, and that answer holds from one message to the next. The second is which of the things they have said matters now, and that answer changes with every message. companion has to get both right. Both answers are claims about real person, and claim about person can only be checked against what that person actually said. Those conversations are private, held by the companies whose products produced them, so the conversations used to test this have been generated instead. RealCompanion1 releases ten real ones, with both answers written down beside them. Figure 1 shows the two questions on one of them. Generated conversations support one kind of measurement. They place fact in dialog and score whether system returns it, which is memorization. Three properties of how they are built set that limit. generated dialog is written around the memory it tests, so nearly every message in it needs the past (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026). prompted persona declares its traits in advance, so question about the person is answered by reading the declaration (Zhang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2025a; Kim et al., 2025). scripted history never revises itself, so nothing said in month nine changes what was established in month four (Jiang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 1Data: https://osf.io/x25kj/?view_only=89106e6a7cbe411b8af9d48b8173c37f. These benchmarks answer both questions before system sees them. The dialog is built so that the past always matters. The persona states in advance what the person is like. Answering those two questions means meeting four challenges. Challenge 1 is knowing when the past matters, since most messages need nothing from earlier. Challenge 2 is knowing what the messages add up to, since who person is emerges across all of them together. Challenge 3 is drawing on everything at once. reply built on the last few messages misses what the person has carried for months. reply built on the facts they stated hands those facts back to them. reply built on trait inferred wrongly is confident and wrong. Challenge 4 is telling whether any of this was done right, and that takes the persons own record. RealCompanion is built from ten people in long-term relationships with AI companions, released with their consent. These conversations were never written to test system, so most messages ask nothing of the past (challenge 1). No one described these people before they spoke, so who they are has to be worked out from what they said (challenge 2). We release five files for each participant. The conversation is the source, and the other four come from it. profile records what the person stated, and persona records how they think, feel and decide. The chat ground truth records what reply had to know and what it should have said, and the question set poses the same decisions as written questions. Together these give system the recent messages, the distant ones, the facts the person stated and the state they are in (challenge 3). Every claim points back at the messages behind it, so reader can check any of it (challenge 4). Three tracks run on these files. The reconstruction track asks system for the profile and persona. The chat track scores its replies to the persons own messages. The question track scores its answers to the written questions. The derivation is done by models and audited by people, and we report how often the two agree (Appendix D). The four derived files divide the work of knowing person. The profile holds every claim the conversation establishes, one record at time, each pointing at the messages behind it. The persona records who they are, how they think and feel, and how they decide. Each entry is filled only where the conversation supports it. Between them, the profile and the persona hold what it takes to understand the person. The question set is written from the profile, so its 3,312 questions across 16 categories reach every claim, fact and trait the conversation established. Every item in the chat ground truth carries reasoning trace, and the trace names what the person was pointing at, where it lives, which messages the reply was built from, and whether those messages support it. label can therefore be contested at the step that produced it. RealCompanion makes all four challenges measurable on relationships that people actually had. We also define the task over any record of person and state seven conditions corpus must meet to measure it (Appendix A).

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND
sections.content: Work on conversational memory has converged on one shape. long history is constructed, question is posed at the end, and system is scored on recovering the fact the question needs. LoCoMo builds very long generated conversations and queries them (Maharana et al., 2024), and LongMemEval scales the context past million tokens (Wu et al., 2024). CloneMem moves to diaries and messages generated from Big Five profiles into multi-year arcs, links each question to evidence units, and reports that flat retrieval beats consolidation-based memory systems (Hu et al., 2026). The shape has produced real machinery, and the memory layers now shipping inside products were tuned against it. It also decides one thing in advance. question states what should be retrieved, so benchmark built from questions never has to judge whether retrieval was warranted. Two benchmarks that test selection directly report how hard it is. CUPID curates histories in which preference holds only in one context, and finds that no model it evaluates exceeds 50% precision at identifying which prior context request depends on (Kim et al., 2025). HorizonBench evolves preferences through mental state graph and reports that all 25 models it evaluates disproportionately select the value from before the change, positioning itself as preparation in advance of longitudinal human data (Li et al., 2026b). Companion applications are setting of their own. person returns to the same agent daily for months, and the relationship is what they are there for. ANCHOR evaluates whether the companion stays itself across 2,008 conversations, 27 personas and three memory configurations, and reports trajectory accuracy of 44.4% with recall of the users state near chance under every configuration (Venkit et al., 2026b). CompanionBench works from de-identified real companion conversations and anchors its rubric in psychological theory, and states directly that 20-turn session cannot reach the depth of disclosure that develops over longer relationship (Liu et al., 2026). Outside machine learning the same relationship is studied through interviews and surveys, which describe how the bond develops over months and document the distress people report when systems behavior changes (Skjuve et al., 2021; Brandtzaeg et al., 2022; Ta et al., 2020; Laestadius et al., 2024). Every one of those studies works from what people say about the interaction afterward. Three efforts remove the substitution at the data. AlpsBench curates 2,500 long-term sequences from WildChat and evaluates seven memory systems on them (Xiao et al., 2026), which makes it the closest prior work to ours on data. PRISM collects feedback from 1,500 people, the largest body of real human preference data in this area (Kirk et al., 2024). OmniBehavior and LUNAR build from real behavioral traces outside conversation (Chen et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a), and OmniBehavior reports that models evaluated on real traces converge toward an average agreeable person and lose the long tail. parallel line supplies written description of the person and scores agreement with it, from PersonaChat through PersonaMem (Zhang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022; Salemi et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025a;b). separate measurement shows that demographics explain 1.5% of the variance in how two people respond (Venkit et al., 2026a). sections.title: 3 THE DATASET
sections.content: The corpus records relationships with an AI companion from the first message to the last. The conversations come from the applications operational store, so every released message stands where the participant sent it. The release is fully anonymized. Every message was rewritten, with direct identifiers replaced by consistent surrogates: the words change, while what the participant said, why they said it and the context it answers are kept. Nobody was recruited to protocol, so the corpus holds what daily use of product produced. Table 2 gives the per-participant composition. RealCompanion is designed per relationship. Each participant is self-contained instance with its own five files, every task is posed within one history, and every result can be reported for one person (Appendix F.6). The two heaviest relationships hold 73% of all messages, nearly three times as many as the other eight combined, and supply the depth longitudinal benchmark exists to test. Depth does not add across people. The eight shorter relationships reflect the lighter use most people make of companion, and it must understand them from far less of what the person has shared. Understanding is not only remembering what they told you, but also reasoning, organizing the memories, and tracing what that says about them. The profile records what someone stated, and every claim in it carries the messages that establish it, confidence, and the window over which it held. Extraction is adversarial toward its own output and throws away more than third of what it proposes, and the claims that later failed audit are kept, so the audit can itself be audited. The persona has no counterpart in prior work, because it holds each reading of person with the messages behind it and stated strength, down to named working hypotheses that carry their grounds and how firmly they are held. Every reference either file makes into the conversation resolves, so reading of person traces back to what was said and can be contested. That is what makes reply in Figure 1 scoreable error. The persona holds only what these ten people revealed. People tell companion about their family, their health, what is worrying them, and almost never state their census category.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Knowing someone shows up in what you can say about them and in what you say to them. The corpus scores both. The question track asks the first, across sixteen kinds of fact authored from the profile, and every item names the messages its answer rests on except the 63 marked unanswerable, which name none by design. The chat track asks the second, and it had to be derived. Its probes are user messages taken verbatim, and its reference reply is written under the recorded context, so no item can depend on anything it does not name. Every label carries the reasoning trace that produced it, written in the same call as the decision it explains, and each stage checks against the conversation, so no claim serves as its own warrant. Appendix specifies the rest: the settings, the schema of each released file, the artifacts of the medium, what the shifted timestamps preserve, the per-subject census behind every macro-average, and how the profiles were built and audited.

sections.title: 4 REASONING OVER CONVERSATIONS TO CONSTRUCT THE GROUND TRUTH
sections.content: Every label here had to be derived, and derived label deserves trust only if reader can check each step. The probes are observed, every label comes from stated procedure that records each decision it makes, and the finished corpus was graded by an audit that procedure does not control. 4.1 PROBES AND ITEMS An item pairs probe with the context correct reply may draw on, reference reply written from that context alone, and the reasoning trace that produced both. The context lists the messages just before the probe, any claims from the profile, and any specific earlier exchanges. Its shape sets the items tier. Preceding messages alone make an item basic, profile claim makes it intermediate, an earlier exchange makes it hard, and an empty context makes it edge, so the tier can be recomputed from the lists without trusting the label. The locus names where the thing the participant is pointing at lives. Of the 1,533 scoreable items, 1,009 point into the current thread and 120 at nothing prior. The other 404 point outside the thread, to profile claim (223), an earlier exchange (116) or the companions own past behavior (65), and on 167 of them the reference reply uses what it cites, which makes them dependent. Appendix D.3 gives the locus distribution by stratum. Every probe is message participant sent, taken verbatim from source, and nothing is rewritten, paraphrased or authored. Choosing which messages to use poses problem, because messages that need the past are rare. In random sample only 3.4% of items need anything outside the current thread, which leaves 40 items to study. The probes come in three strata, and each answers one question. The proportional stratum is that random sample, 1,169 scoreable items drawn from every participant, and it alone answers how often the past is needed (condition V3 of Appendix A.4). The enriched stratum answers what system does when the past is needed. The abstention control answers whether system holds back when nothing is needed. Its 434 session openers need nothing prior, and benchmark on which retrieval helps cannot detect system that retrieves too much. 4.2 TRACED REASONING Figure 2 shows the five stages. Stage resolves what the probe points at and names the store it would live in. Stage retrieves candidate records for that referent and checks each against source, dropping what fails. Stage assigns the tier and category by one of nineteen fixed rules and records the rule that fired. Stage writes the reference reply and names the messages it rests on. Stage checks that the reply is supported by its evidence and that the category fits, and demotes the item when either check fails. Each stage reads only what the stages before it wrote, and writes its decision and its reason in the same call, so no rationale is reconstructed after the decision it explains. That record is the items reasoning trace. Appendix D.1 states what each stage may and may not revise. label can go wrong in three ways, and the order of the stages closes each one. The first is invented evidence. By Stage B, an invented profile claim cannot confirm probe and enter the gold as memory system is expected to retrieve (V5). The second is reply that depends on something the item does not name. By Stage D, the context is sufficient by construction, and the gap between the oracle condition and any retriever measures retrieval alone (V1). The recorded grounding confirms it. Because this reply is constructed, the reply the participant actually received is kept as well, as the message after each probe in source, so every result can be re-run against it. sections.content: RealCompanion benchmarks the two questions about person that Section 1 separates. The first is who the participant is. The reconstruction track tests it: system reads the participants full history and writes the profile and persona files. The second is which of the things they have said bears on the message in front of system. The chat and question tracks test it by scoring whether system reaches for the past at all, which earlier messages it finds, and what its reply makes of them. The reasoning trace of Section 4 records how each chat label was decided, and the chat track reads its outputs: the reference set, whether memory is needed, the tier and the reference reply. sections.title: 6 RESULTS
sections.content: Every rate below divides by stated denominator. The proportional stratum (1,169 scoreable probes of 1,227) carries every population rate on the chat track. The enriched stratum (364 of 373) is census of the deep-history items, so it supports conditional statements and no rates. The abstention control (434 cold opens) is scored only for abstention. Two readings run throughout: the recorded reading keeps all 404 memory-bearing probes, 40 proportional and 364 enriched. The strict reading removes the 154 whose referent is visible on screen (Appendix C.7). Each result is reported by population, because pooled number reports the corpus composition of as much as the capability (Proposition 2). Memory is required far less often than benchmark construction implies. On the natural-rate stratum, 3.4% [2.5, 4.6] of the messages participants sent carry verified memory demand under the recorded reading and 1.3% [0.8, 2.1] under the strict one. Verification is monotone, so each of these bounds the true rate from below (Proposition 1), and two procedures over the 11,369 participant messages outside that sample agree. The census of Section 4 gives 3.2% [2.9, 3.5] and re-reading of it under the Stage instruction gives 1.73% [1.45, 2.06] (Appendix F.1). The requirement is also uneven. Three of the ten participants contribute no memory-bearing item under the recorded reading, and five under the strict one. Memory demand is property of relationship depth. When message draws on the past, the material it needs usually sits far back. The furthest message memory-bearing probe requires sits median of 2,157 messages back, with an upper quartile of 5,114 and maximum of 12,542. Even the nearest required message sits median of 450 messages back. The length of the relationship fixes the horizon system must cover. Locating that material defeats the scorers memory system usually reaches for. Table 4 reports how often required message appears in the top five for the distant items. Recency, the order sliding context window imposes, finds one for 0.022 of them against 0.005 for random ranking, and for none once on-screen referents are removed (Appendix E.2). Lexical matching finds one eleven times as often, at 0.248, and still misses three in four. The broken oracle scores 0.000 throughout, as control must. Pooling reverses this order. Over the 1,477 chat probes with reference set, of which 72.6% are answerable from the recent thread, recency finds required message for 0.959 of them and lexical matching for 0.236. Lexical matching barely moves between the two populations, while recency falls by factor of forty. pooled retrieval score reports the composition of the corpus. Coverage of the required message rises with the context budget, from 0.109 at 8k tokens to 0.453 at 128k and 1.000 at one million, where every history fits (Figure 4, Appendix F.3). What model does with the context it is given is separate question, and the next three results answer it. Supplying context helps, and most of the help reaches probes that need no memory. Table 5 reports mean content match, on 0 to 2 scale, over the 1,533 scoreable probes of both strata. Every contrast below is mean of per-probe differences. sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: RealCompanion releases ten real relationships between people and an AI companion, and every chat item carries the reasoning trace that produced it, checked against the conversation it came from. The past is rarely needed and, when it is, far away: 3.4% of sampled messages reach outside the current thread, median of 2,157 messages back, and the demand concentrates in the longest relationships. Where it is needed, supplying the recorded evidence raises content match by 0.455, yet no system we evaluate decides when to reach back, and no detector we tried tells the two situations apart on real messages. On who the person is, three agent systems reconstruct the persona with the same F1 at 31-fold difference in cost, and all three add about seventy to eighty further fields for every hundred they recover. Unlike an authored corpus, RealCompanion knows how often memory is actually required.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Language models are research instruments in this work, and each use is disclosed with its check. They run stages A, and of the derivation (Section 4), generate and judge the replies of Section 5, audit both tracks, and are the systems the reconstruction track evaluates; every per-stage decision ships in the released items. They also produced parts of the released data: the anonymization rewrote every message with model, the question track was built with one, and the persona and profile layers were generated by model pipeline and then reviewed by hand (Appendices D.8 and H). We did not take their output on trust. Twenty-six release gates and five families of mechanical check run over the corpus without model, an independent model graded what the derivation produced, and where an instrument overstated itself we report it. We also used AI assistants to write and debug code, give feedback on experimental design, help interpret results, search for related work, check references, and draft and edit prose. Every number was recomputed by script, every sentence was read and revised by an author, and the authors take full responsibility for the content.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: The conversations are by ten people using companion application for their own purposes; all consented to research use and release. Every released file is anonymized: account identifiers, contact details, names and named entities are replaced with consistent surrogates across all five files, and what remains is what each participant said and the context it answers, in rewritten words, with the interaction structure, session rhythm and communicative style on which this research depends. The corpus contains material falling within the special categories of Article 9 of the GDPR (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016), and necessarily so: reply that ignores what someone has said about their health is not the correct reply, and benchmark that stripped such material would measure different task while claiming to measure this one. Processing rests on each participants explicit consent to research use and release, the basis Article 9(2)(a) provides for special-category data. The study and the release were approved by the data operators internal ethics committee under its privacy policy and terms of service; that committee is not independent of the operator, and no institutional review board was involved. Given sample of participants writing and the ten released histories, stylometric classifier using no content words matches them at 83.0% and language model at 98.0%, against chance rate of 10%; the statistical adversary needs volume, and the language model does not. Removing identifiers does not remove authorship, and that is property of conversational text. We report the measurement because corpus described as anonymized without one is describing an assumption. The release terms prohibit profiling, identifying or targeting any individual, and any commercial use (Appendix H.5). sections.title: A THE EVALUATION TASK
sections.content: Section 2 states the task informally. This appendix gives it formally: the objects an instance supplies (A.1), how the three decisions are scored and aggregated (A.2), what follows for measurement when the demand rate is low (A.3), and the conditions corpus must meet to count as an instance at all (A.4). The definitions are stated over an arbitrary subject record, because RealCompanion is one instance of the task. A.1 SUBJECT RECORDS AND PROBES The task is defined over record of one person, independently of how that record was obtained. subject record is pair (M, S). The stream = (m1, . . . , mN ) is sequence of messages ordered in time, each carrying sender, timestamp, and its text, with senders partitioned into those attributable to the person and those attributable to anything else. The family = {S1, . . . , SL} is finite set of stores, each set of records derived from and each standing for one place system might look for something the person said before; for RealCompanion, = 2, the profile claims and, as the episode store, the messages of themselves. An instance of the task is finite collection of subject records together with the annotation defined below. sections.title: B RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Section 2 states the position, and Table 1 gives the comparison. Personalization has no observable ground truth, so the field makes three substitutions. description stands in for the person, an authored question stands in for the moment that needs memory, and models judgment stands in for the target. Each substitution has cost that can be measured. This appendix sets out the three (B.1), what they cost (B.2), the attempts to remove them (B.3), adjacent work on memory systems and rationales (B.4), what releasing the alternative requires (B.5), and the criteria behind the table (B.6). B.1 THREE SUBSTITUTIONS description stands in for the person. The word persona entered dialogue research through PersonaChat (Zhang et al., 2018), where crowd-workers were given short sets of persona sentences and asked to converse while conditioned on them. It solved real problem, since model with no representation of its user produces generic replies. persona in this tradition is an input the experimenter controls, and no reply can contradict it, because nothing outside the description exists to check it against. Multi-session chat (Xu et al., 2022) extended the format past single conversation, collecting dialogues that resume across three to five sessions and carrying summaries forward, which made long-range consistency measurable. The personas are still supplied in advance, and the time between sessions is simulated, with workers told to write as if one to seven hours or one to seven days had passed. What accumulates is record of task performed on schedule. The tradition now operates at industrial scale. Nemotron-Personas-USA (Meyer & Corneil, 2025) releases million synthetic personas aligned to real-world demographic distributions, each set of prose facets covering profession, sports, arts, travel and cuisine, alongside demographic fields. Two works measure what the assumption behind such personas costs. Venkit et al. (2026a) administer 141-item sociopsychological protocol to 124 people and report that demographics explain roughly 1.5% of the variance in how similarly two people respond, so persona assembled from demographic attributes is very nearly unrelated to the person it describes. Neplenbroek et al. (2026) append high-stakes advice questions to 8,011 PRISM conversations (Kirk et al., 2024) and 26,521 from the Community Alignment Dataset (Zhang et al., 2025a), and find that conversation topic predicts models advice better than inferred sociodemographics, which models infer poorly in any case. What system adapts to, when it adapts to conversation, is what the conversation is about.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: An authored question stands in for the moment that needs memory. Work on conversational memory has converged on common shape. long interaction history is constructed, question is posed at the end, and the system is scored on whether it recovers the fact needed to answer. LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) builds very long machine-generated conversations and queries them in the third person. LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) scales the context past million tokens and targets factual recall across sessions. CloneMem (Hu et al., 2026) argues that conversation captures only fragments of life and moves to diaries and messages generated top-down from Big Five profiles into multi-year arcs. It links each question to evidence units, defines eight reasoning categories including unanswerable items, and reports that flat retrieval beats consolidation-based memory because summarization severs the link to the original traces. Transplanted into conversation, the shape brings an assumption with it. question states what should be retrieved, so the benchmark decides for the system whether retrieval was warranted, and it scores finding the right material and using it well as single outcome. The personalization line adopts the same shape while varying what the question is about. LaMP (Salemi et al., 2024) formulates personalization as seven classification and generation tasks over public user histories, within single message. PersonaMem (Jiang et al., 2025a) builds 180 simulated interaction histories from PersonaHub seeds (Ge et al., 2024) and asks model to identify the most suitable response given the current state of user profile. PersonaMem-v2 (Jiang et al., 2025b) scales to 1,000 personas and shifts to implicit preferences that surface as side effects of ordinary requests, where the models it evaluates reach 37% to 55%. CUPID (Kim et al., 2025) curates 756 interaction histories in which preference holds only in specific context, and reports that no model it evaluates exceeds 50% precision and 65% recall at identifying which prior context new request depends on. recurring finding across this line is that models fail to update. HorizonBench (Li et al., 2026b) constructs 4,245 items from 360 simulated users whose preferences evolve through mental state graph, and reports that all 25 models it evaluates disproportionately select the pre-evolution value. Its authors state that whether the failure holds at the same severity in naturalistic interaction is unresolved, and position the benchmark as preparation in advance of longitudinal human data. In the companion setting, ANCHOR (Venkit et al., 2026b) evaluates persona collapse and behavioral drift over 2,008 conversations spanning 27 personas, nine interaction schedules and three memory configurations. Trajectory accuracy averages 44.4%, recall of the users state sits near four-option chance, and no memory configuration resolves either. ANCHOR asks whether the companion stays itself. The 65 probes in this corpus whose locus is the companion ask the same question of an interaction that happened. models judgment stands in for the target. Scoring open-ended responses with language model was introduced at scale by MT-Bench and Chat-bot Arena (Zheng et al., 2023), which also documented the failure modes: position bias, verbosity bias, and preference for the judges own outputs. Those biases are tolerable when the quantity being judged is otherwise observable. In personalization the target is unobserved, so the judge substitutes for it. recent survey of personalized agents names this among the open problems, alongside the reliance on synthetic users (Xu et al., 2026). Our design keeps this substitution and bounds it three ways. The generator is held constant across all five conditions, so any preference for its style applies uniformly and cannot order them. The five candidates for probe are shuffled and scored in one call, which removes position effects and drift in the judges use of the scale. Evidence coverage, which uses no judge, is reported alongside content match as check that shares none of its failure modes. B.2 WHAT THE SUBSTITUTIONS COST The three substitutions are not independent. The second, authoring the probe, is load-bearing. It removes three decisions from the task at once, and each removal is visible as gap in the literature. Restraint. question announces that something must be looked up, so benchmark built from questions cannot score system for deciding whether to look. The methods that learn this decision learn it from the question. Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) trains reflection tokens that let model call for passages on demand, Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al., 2024) trains classifier over query complexity and routes between no retrieval, single-step retrieval and multi-step retrieval, and Mallen et al. (2023) retrieve only for questions about less popular entities. All three read signal the question supplies.

sections.content: SQuAD 2.0 (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) made not answering first-class label by adding over 50,000 questions with no answer in the passage, and the idea carried into conversational memory as the unanswerable categories of CloneMem and of our question track. The conversational analogue is message that calls for no memory at all, which describes most messages. That case cannot be constructed by authoring, because an author writing probe that requires nothing has written nothing worth scoring. Locus. Before conversational query can be retrieved against, its references have to be resolved, and conversational search has long studied that operation. QReCC (Anantha et al., 2021) pairs 14,000 conversations with rewrites that message context-dependent question into standalone one, and Mo et al. (2025) survey the line. That work presupposes question to rewrite. Stage (Section 4) performs the same operation on an ordinary message and records the outcome as locus, which states where the referent lives. The label exists here because the probes are ordinary messages. Reach. An author who knows the answer places its evidence wherever the question needs it, so the distance between probe and evidence is design choice, and Liu et al. (2024) show that where evidence sits in context changes whether model uses it. Real conversation produces bimodal distribution instead. Probes that point into the current thread reach back median of 2 messages and at most 15. Probes that point outside it reach median of 450 messages to the nearest cited message and 2,157 to the furthest, and as far as 12,542. B.3 ATTEMPTS TO REMOVE THEM Recent work removes one substitution at time. Each effort keeps the others, and which one it keeps is the informative part. AlpsBench (Xiao et al., 2026) curates 2,500 long-term interaction sequences from WildChat, corpus of real exchanges between people and assistants, and evaluates seven memory systems on extraction, update, retrieval, and utilization. It is the closest prior work to ours on data, and it removes the first substitution. It keeps the second, since its evaluation queries are synthesized by language model from the dialogues. Its data also records different activity. WildChat users bring tasks to general assistant, so even its longest sequences are series of requests. CompanionBench (Liu et al., 2026) draws on de-identified real companion conversations and anchors its rubric in psychological theory. It removes the first substitution at collection and restores it at release, since it releases rewritten persona pairs and evaluates single 20-message sessions against simulator. Its authors state that such sessions cannot reach the depth of disclosure that develops over longer relationship. PRISM (Kirk et al., 2024) collects feedback from 1,500 people across 75 countries and is the largest body of real human preference data in this area. It is the one effort that removes the third substitution as well as the first, since its judgments come from people. Its unit is rated single-session conversation, so it establishes what people prefer and leaves open what system should remember. Two efforts outside conversation turn to real behavior. OmniBehavior (Chen et al., 2026a) assembles user-simulation benchmark from real behavioral traces and describes itself as the first built wholly from real-world data, and LUNAR (Zhang et al., 2026b) builds personalization tasks from app behavior logs through synthesis pipeline grounded in real behavioral patterns. Neither is conversational, so neither poses the decision this paper is about: trace records what person did, and simulator is scored against the next action. What OmniBehavior reports is nonetheless the strongest external statement of why records of this kind are needed. Evaluated on real traces, models converge toward an average and agreeable person, showing hyperactivity and homogenized personas, and losing individual differences and long-tail behavior. That is failure written corpus cannot exhibit, because written corpus has no long tail: its users were composed, and nothing is in them that an author did not put there. B.4 ADJACENT WORK parallel line of engineering builds the systems these benchmarks measure, and its design choices constrain evaluation from the other direction. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) treats the context window as level in memory hierarchy and pages material in and out of external storage under model control. Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) maintains memory stream retrieved by recency, importance,

AI Persona (Wang et al., 2024) carries this furthest for user modeling, maintaining lifelong profile that an optimizer updates every few sessions without retraining; it is the closest prior work to the profile file we release, and differs in that its claims are not bound to the messages that established them. The last property decides what benchmark can measure. system that stores messages can be scored by identifier match against gold set. system that stores distilled statements cannot, because there is no identifier to match, which is why Section 5 defines judged recall alongside the exact one and reports the two separately. We evaluate three of these systems as deployed products, since the write policy is part of what is being measured and re-implementation would replace it with ours. Attaching rationales to labels has long history, with e-SNLI (Camburu et al., 2018) as the canonical example: annotators assign label and then write why. Those rationales are written after the label by the annotator who assigned it, so rationale cannot disagree with its label. CloneMems evidence units and CUPIDs preference checklists are partial instances of the same idea, since both expose what gold answer rests on. Neither records how the gold answer was reached. Each item here carries reasoning trace instead, recording the procedure that produced the label, the intermediate results that were checked, and the points where check failed and the label was revised. stage can contradict the stage before it, and on 685 of the 1,533 scoreable items, 44.7%, the final tier differs from the pre-verification signal. The practical difference is what reader can do with disagreement. rationale can be judged unconvincing, which leaves the label standing. reasoning trace can be rejected at named stage, which identifies every other item that stage decided the same way. B.5 WHAT RELEASING THE ALTERNATIVE REQUIRES The three substitutions were forced by access, so removing them means releasing material that was withheld for reason. Two works of literature state what that costs and what it is worth. Because memory accumulates personal information, parallel line asks what system should decline to use. ConfAIde (Mireshghallah et al., 2024) and CIMemories (Mireshghallah et al., 2026) apply contextual integrity to model outputs, showing that appropriateness depends on the recipient and the purpose. CIMemories shapes our design for methodological reason. It argues that leakage and utility must be scored on the same items. The same logic governs retrieval. memory system that surfaces nothing never intrudes and never helps, which is why restraint and recall are scored on the same probes and why the abstention controls in Section 4 exist. The release itself is held to the same standard: Appendix reports what an adversary recovers from the files alongside what the files still support. Outside machine learning, researchers study these relationships directly. Interview studies of companion application users describe how the relationship develops over months and what people come to expect from it (Skjuve et al., 2021), and follow-on work examines how users construe the bond, including where they treat it as friendship and where they do not (Brandtzaeg et al., 2022). Thematic analyses document the social support people report receiving (Ta et al., 2020), and grounded-theory work on emotional dependence documents the harms, including distress when the systems behavior changes (Laestadius et al., 2024). Every one of these studies works from what people say about the interaction, through interviews, surveys, app reviews and forum posts. That is the constraint that produced the three substitutions, met by different field and answered different way. Where machine learning generated substitute for the interaction, this literature asked people to recall it. This release supplies the interaction itself, which is why every profile claim cites the messages behind it and every chat item carries its reasoning trace. What the corpus cannot supply is what these studies supply. It contains no participants account, and ten people who chose one product are not sample of any population. conversation between particular person and an agent over months exists once, belongs to that person, and cannot be regenerated if the release is wrong. That asymmetry is why Appendix measures what an adversary recovers, and why the Ethics Statement states the basis on which the material may be used. Removing the substitutions is question of consent before it is question of scale.

sections.content: Section 3 describes the corpus; this appendix specifies it. It covers the application the conversations came from (C.1), the schema of the five released files (C.2), the features of the medium reader would otherwise misread (C.3), what timestamps do and do not mean (C.4), the per-subject census behind every macro-average (C.5), how the profile and persona were built and audited (C.6), and the invariants reader can check without trusting us (C.7). C.1 THE SETTING The corpus comes from an internal AI-companion application in which user keeps persistent friendship-style companion. The companion has name, mood, an outfit, and the application layers daily streak, habit tracker, snack economy and several mini-games over an open-ended chat. Two properties of this setting matter for the benchmark. The traffic is ordinary contact, made of greetings, accounts of day, running jokes and long stretches in which nothing is asked. The companion also opens the exchange as often as the participant does, speaking first on 217 of the 430 active days against 207 for participant and 6 for the application, so probe often sits inside conversation the participant did not start. Both properties are costly to script, and corpus written for evaluation rarely has either. The release contains 27,218 messages across ten subjects and 430 subject-days. How that divides between the subjects, and what the derived layers add to it, is in Appendix C.5; Table 2 gives the per-subject totals. Measured with the tokenizer released alongside the corpus, the transcripts total 1,643,158 tokens, or 60.37 per message.

sections.content: C.4 TIMESTAMPS AND OBSERVATION WINDOWS Timestamps were shifted by per-subject offset, uniform across every date and timestamp belonging to that subject, deterministic in the subject identifier, with magnitude between 60 and 359 days and sign that varies by subject. Time of day is carried through unchanged. Every interval is therefore exact, so active spans, gaps between sessions, session rhythm and the hour at which subject writes are all preserved and can be measured from the release. Day of the week survives only for participant whose offset happens to be multiple of seven, and reader cannot tell which participants those are, so the release supports no claim about weekday or weekend behavior. An observation window runs from subjects first message to their last authored turn. It closes on turn the subject wrote, because the companion may send further messages after someone has stopped replying, and counting those would credit the relationship with days in which the subject was absent. Both bounds are recoverable from the released timestamps, so the window is re-computable. Its length is the number of calendar days it touches, counting both endpoints. Windows span 36 to 120 days, of which 9 to 111 carry activity. Because the offset above is uniform within subject, the length of window is exact even though its position in the calendar is not. C.5 PER-SUBJECT CENSUS Table 2 is re-computable from the release, and this is what each column counts. Span is the length of the observation window defined in Appendix C.4, and Active days is the number of calendar days on which any message was sent. Messages counts every message regardless of sender, 12,795 of them the participants own. Chat items counts scoreablerows in the proportional and enriched strata, and Question items counts question rows not withdrawn, of which 77 are. The ten subjects differ by two orders of magnitude. The smallest contributes 115 turns over 9 active days and the largest 12,627 over 95, and density varies independently of volume: one subject is active on 111 of 111 consecutive days, another on 9 days spread across 36. The derived layers scale with the transcript, from 22 profile claims to 1,363, but one of them conspicuously does not. Persona emptiness is almost flat across the corpus: the subject with 115 turns leaves 26 of 39 slots empty and the subject with 12,627 leaves 19. hundredfold increase in what someone said fills seven further slots. The sparsity reported in Section 3 is therefore not an artifact of thin data, and Appendix C.6 gives the breakdown by slot type. The concentration decides how results are aggregated. Two subjects supply 73% of the turns, so figure pooled over items estimates how those two behave, which is why every rate in this paper is reported pooled over items with its macro beside it, as Appendix A.2 specifies. One consequence must be stated. Under the strict reading of Appendix D.4 five subjects contribute no memory-bearing probes at all, so quantities conditioned on memory demand are macro-averaged over the five that do and not over ten, and on the proportional stratum those five contribute between one and seven probes each. Table 14 gives the counts. Intervals on those quantities are correspondingly wide and are reported as they come out. C.6 PROFILE AND PERSONA CONSTRUCTION Extraction is adversarial toward its own output, and most of what it proposes it throws away. Of 7,176 candidate claims, 2,654 were dropped for cause: 1,508 cited no evidence at all, 693 were ungrounded in the evidence they did cite, and 453 were unreliable given it, rejection rate of 37.0%. further 1,212 were merged into existing claims as duplicates, and later enrichment pass over the same conversations restored material the first pass had missed, leaving the 3,580 claims that ship, 3,579 of them carrying evidence. Every drop reason is released. The rejected material is informative, because attributes that were never stated and aspirations recorded as facts are exactly the errors that would otherwise become gold answers. later audit re-examined the surviving claims against source, judged 3,378 of the 3,580, and recorded each verdict on the claim itself; Table 15 gives the distribution. Claims the audit could not support are retained, so that the audit is itself auditable: reader who disagrees with verdict has the claim, its evidence and the verdict in front of them. Eighteen further markers record what was done to individual claims, among them 538 rejudged after an error in source was corrected, 500 re-filed against normalized entity name, 290 with speaker attribution fixed, 135 with journal evidence

sections.content: Section 4 describes what chat item records and why its labels can be trusted. This appendix gives the full derivation and what it rejected. It covers the five stages (D.1), probe selection (D.2), the three labels and their recomputability (D.3), the judgment of whether referent was already on screen (D.4), the rows withdrawn, demoted or repaired (D.5), the independent audit (D.6), the release gates (D.7), and the question track (D.8). D.1 THE FIVE PHASES Derivation alternates between proposing and checking. Stages and put something forward, stages and check it against source, and stage applies fixed rule to what survives. The arrangement is what gives the error direction, because no phase downstream of check can restore what the check removed, so failure of the pipeline makes an item look less demanding than it is. Table 16 states what each phase writes and what it is permitted to revise. Every phase records its own reasoning in the item, so reader can locate disagreement at the phase that caused it. Phase Writes May revise C referent_text, locus rationaleB tier, category, ruleC gold_response, grounding_dayids ok, category_ok nothing; it is the first statement the reference set, by removing entries whose evidence does not verify; it may never add one nothing; both are functions of the context shape left behind nothing; it conditions on the context left behind whether the item ships: failure is returned for repair or withdrawn Table 16: What each phase writes. Phase resolves what the probe is pointing at. It records the referring expression verbatim in referent_text and names the store the referent would live in, and it is permitted to be wrong, because nothing has been checked yet. Phase is the check. For each reference proposed it retrieves the candidate records and tests them against source, and where the evidence does not verify it removes the reference. reference that survives has been matched to turns that exist and precede the probe. tier therefore falls only when stage has removed evidence (Appendix D.5). Phase assigns the tier and the category by rule, from the context shape that survived B. Nineteen rules cover the corpus, and the item records which one fired in ruleC. Because reads only the shape and never the prose, the tier is function of the three context lists and not judgment, which is what makes it re-computable by reader and what produces the exact correspondence reported in Appendix D.3. It is also why cannot demote an item directly: removes evidence, and then reads different shape and assigns different tier. Phase writes the reference reply and records which turns it rests on. The test that matters is containment: the grounding must lie inside the recent window, the surviving references, and the probe itself, since gold response is entitled to use the turn it is answering and the turns already on screen. Grounding is recorded on 1,342 of the 1,533 scoreable rows, and on none of them does it name turn outside that set, which is the verification of the sufficiency condition of Appendix A.4. It re-reads the probe, the gold, and the assigned category together and either passes the item or sends it back, and items that cannot be repaired are withdrawn. Every shipped row therefore carries ok and category_ok set true, on all 1,533, and this should not be read as evidence that the annotation is correct. It is property of what ships: the field records that an item survived its own pipeline, not that an independent reader agrees with it. What speaks to correctness is the audit of Appendix D.6, which was run afterwards and against different questions. D.2 PROBE SELECTION AND THE THREE STRATA Probes are user turns, and the sampling frame is every user turn in the corpus. Turns were drawn from buckets by routing heuristic scored on the turn and its neighborhood, and the bucket each row came from is recorded in signals.hint. That field is deliberately never recomputed. It states which bucket the sampler drew from, before any phase had checked anything, so the released item preserves what the sampler believed alongside what the derivation found. reader can therefore audit the sample as well as the labels. The chat file carries three strata, and they answer different questions. The proportional stratum is 1,227 rows, 1,169 of them scoreable, drawn between 32 and 326 per participant without conditioning on whether message needs memory. It alone has denominator, so every rate that describes the traffic is computed on it and nowhere else. The enriched stratum is 373 rows, 364 scoreable, found by running stage over all 11,581 unused user messages and keeping what stage verified. All 364 are memory-bearing by construction, so the stratum supplies power and no rate, since comparisons conditioned on memory demand would otherwise rest on the 40 such rows the proportional stratum contains. The abstention control is 434 session openers with empty context lists, scored apart and entering no rate. The census also corroborates the proportional estimate: stage verified distant referent on 3.7% of the 11,369 messages stage classified, against 3.4% in the proportional stratum. Because the bucket is preserved, the sample yields measurement nobody designed it to yield. Table 17 crosses the bucket row was drawn from against the tier phase assigned after verification. They agree on 848 of the 1,532 rows carrying comparable bucket, so the heuristic was wrong 44.6% of the time; one further row carries non-tier bucket value and is excluded. The failures are not symmetric. Of the 97 turns the sampler was most confident carried distant memory demand, 10 survived verification as hard, and 72 turned out to need nothing beyond the current thread. Of the 386 it routed as intermediate, 88 were. Of the 173 it routed as needing nothing, 63 turned out to need specific earlier exchange. sections.content: E.3 RETRIEVAL BASELINES Each method returns 20 messages from the pool and is scored at ranks 1, 5, and 20 and by reciprocal rank. RANDOM draws 20 messages from the pool under fixed seed. RECENCY returns the 20 messages immediately preceding the probe, either sender. RECENCY-USER returns the 20 preceding user messages, which separates adjacency from who was speaking. ORACLE returns the items own gold set, ordered by weight, with recent context and primary references above supporting ones, truncated at 20; it falls short of perfect recall on items whose gold set exceeds the cut. BM25 is the only method that reads the probes content. On the question track, the pool is the participants whole history, since question is posed over the record, and evidence messages carry the primary weight. BM25 uses k1 = 1.5, = 0.75 and idf = log(cid:0)1 + (N df + 0.5)/(df + 0.5)(cid:1). The index unit is one turn, both senders, and each participants history is indexed once. Text is lower-cased and tokenized on [a-z0-9]+ with tokens shorter than three characters and fixed 62-word stop list discarded. The query is the probe text unmodified. The top 40 are retrieved, filtered to positions preceding the probe, and the first 20 kept. All values are macro-averaged over participants. E.4 THE RESPONSE JUDGE One judge at temperature zero scores all five candidate replies for probe in single call, so the conditions are ranked against one another, and no drift in the judges use of the scale can order them. It is shown the probe, the full gold response, the text of the messages the item records as required at 200 characters each with an explicit placeholder where there are none, and the five candidates at 400 characters each, labeled by condition. It is not shown the recent thread, the profile, the persona, the reasoning trace, the participant, or what the condition labels mean. It returns three fields: content_match on three-point scale against the gold, used_memory recording whether the reply asserts specific detail about the past that the probe did not supply, correct or not, and restraint recording whether the reply volunteers no such detail at all. The judges agreement with human adjudication was measured on 100 probes, each carrying five replies, read blind. On used_memory and restraint it agrees on 90.6% of replies, κ = 0.804. On the three-point content_match it agrees exactly on 77.4% and is never wrong by two points, κ = 0.545 and 0.606 under linear weighting; where it differs it is harsher than the reader, lower on 81 replies and higher on 32. The contrasts this paper relies on reproduce. On the same sample the reader and the judge put C2 above C1 by 0.13 and 0.14, C3 below C1 by 0.15 and 0.19, C4 below C1 by 0.05 and 0.09, and C1 above C0 by 0.22 and 0.24. systematic severity that applies to all five conditions cannot reorder them. Two of the correspondences are approximations and are stated as such. system in the ablation never emits retrieval decision, so its restraint decision is read off its reply: reply that volunteers detail about the past is treated as having chosen to retrieve. Likewise the appropriate application rate is read from whether the reply asserts past detail the probe did not supply, correct or not, because the ablation supplies context and no system returns retrieved set; whether the detail is right is left to content match. Evidence coverage exists because every other response-side number depends on the judge of Appendix E.4, whose agreement on the graded scale is the weaker of its two measurements. It uses no model, shares none of the judges failure modes, and moves in the same direction on the same comparisons, which is the closest thing to validation the response side currently has. It is weak measure taken alone, since reply can repeat the words of an evidence turn without using it, and is reported only alongside content match. sections.title: F ADDITIONAL RESULTS
sections.content: Section 6 reports one figure per claim. This appendix reports the rest: every method on every subset, every condition under every reading, and the per-subject values behind each macro-average. It covers how the demand rate was estimated (F.1), retrieval in full (F.2), context-window coverage (F.3), the ablation in full (F.4), selectivity and detection (F.5), the per-subject tables (F.6), and the deployed systems (F.7). F.1 ESTIMATING THE DEMAND RATE The demand rate π of (2) is the quantity every other rate in this paper is conditioned on, and Proposition 1 makes single measurement of it lower bound. Three procedures were therefore run, with different denominators and different failure modes, and this subsection gives each. The first is census. Phase was run over every user turn in the corpus, not over sample, so memory-bearing turn can be missed only if the resolver fails on it, never because it was not looked at. sections.title: G PERSONA AND PROFILE RECONSTRUCTION
sections.content: The reconstruction track asks system to read subjects full history in source and build the persona and profile layers from it (schemas in Appendix C.2). The persona holds Big Five levels, demographics, behavioral quirks, fifteen prose sections and personality dimensions; the profile holds identity fields, speaking style, Big Five levels, personality dimensions, categorized facts and named entities. The release pipeline builds both from the history in pieces: the persona chain distills it one day at time into store of claims, and the profile generators read it in windows. The agentic method instead reads the whole history in one pass, with no day slicing and no claim store, and every extracted item must cite the subjects own turns. Three systems each ran three times on each of the ten subjects. G.1 TASK AND SCOPE Subjects. Ten subjects, U01U10, with 115 to 12,627 turns each  (Table 2)  . Each turn has an id of the form dayN-M and sender: user (the subject), companion or app. profile claim may rest on something the companion said if the subject ratified it, by affirming it, repeating it or building on it as settled; silence does not count, and the evidence cited is the subjects ratifying turn. Token counts here are the builders estimate, characters 4 over message text, about 20% above the cl100k_base counts of Section 3; they run from 2,743 to 1,023,911 per subject  (Table 43)  , and the transcript rendered for the prompts is 626% larger. GT fills 239 persona and 476 profile fields across the ten subjects. The two longest subjects hold 83% of all transcript tokens but only 18% of the scored persona fields and 39% of the scored profile fields, so pooled scores weight subjects by fields, and G.6 reports each subject. Scope. All ten subjects are scored, by all three systems in both layers, and every pooled score covers all ten. history too long for one context is read in two halves (G.2). Ground truth. GT is the released persona and profile layers, which the release pipeline generated and the authors then reviewed by hand. The persona chains late stages read fixed-size inputs, which shrinks the persona GT on long histories (G.6). The profile GT for U02U10 was built on the pre-anonymization history and repaired against the release, and unlike the runs it also cites companion turns (1,034 of its 7,315 citations). G.2 SYSTEMS AND SETTINGS Systems. Each system ran three independent runs per subject and layer, sharing no state. Claude Opus 5.5 ran as agent workflows with file tools and 1M-token context, with the history inline (U01 U07) or in files each agent reads in full (U08U10); contexts near the window were auto-compacted, and on U09, 23 of the 27 persona readers and 4 of the 6 profile agents answered from 1738k-token summary, as did one U10 agent. Codex GPT-5.6-sol ran through the Responses API, one request per call with the history inline, sent by separate runner, not audited here, that applies the same prompts and edits; single request cannot be compacted, and the largest was about 597k tokens (U09). sections.title: H DATASHEET
sections.content: This datasheet follows the structure of Gebru et al. (2021). H.1 MOTIVATION The corpus was assembled to measure whether system knows when to remember and what to remember, on conversations nobody wrote for that purpose. No existing corpus pairs real longitudinal conversation with per-item record of whether memory was required, and Appendix B.1 sets out why: the records are private, so the field substituted written users, authored questions and model judgment for them. The benchmark is the narrowest use of the result; Appendix describes the others. Assembly, annotation and release were carried out by the authors. H.2 COMPOSITION What an instance is. The release has two kinds. turn is one message in conversation, with its sender, timestamp, text and marker where media accompanied it. An item is one evaluation instance: probe turn, the context correct reply may draw on, reference reply, and the record of how those were decided. How many. Ten subjects contribute 27,218 turns across 430 subject-days, of which 12,795 are the subjects, 14,329 the companions and 94 the applications, totaling 1.64 million tokens. The chat track ships 2,034 rows, 1,600 sampled and 434 abstention, of which 1,967 are scoreable. The question track ships 3,312 items, of which 3,235 are scoreable. The profile layer holds 3,580 claims and the persona layer 390 content slots per the schemas of Appendix C.2. Sample or population. For each of the ten subjects the corpus contains every turn from the first message to the last, so it is complete for those subjects and is not sample of any population. The probe strata are described in Appendix D.2; only the proportional stratum supports rate. Labels. Each item carries whether retrieval beyond the recent window is required, which store holds the needed record, tier and category recomputable from the context lists, reference reply, and five-phase derivation recording how each was reached. What is missing, and why. Media content is not released, only marker that media were present. Model replies generated for comparison and never shown to subject, and messages emitted inside in-application games, were removed before delivery, leaving 3,273 vacant slots in the identifier space. Sixty-seven chat rows are withdrawn and ship without probe text, each with its reason. Timestamps carry per-subject offset, so intervals are exact and calendar position is not.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Relationships between instances. Every claim in every derived layer cites turn identifiers in the underived layer: 18,983 citations, none of which fails to resolve. Appendix C.7 reports the check. Splits. There is no canonical train and test split, and none should be inferred from the strata, which partition by how probes were selected. Errors and noise. The chat tracks independent audit is in Appendix D.6; the question track carries content defect rate of 3.8% [3.2, 4.6] after four repair passes, given in Appendix D.8. The profile ships 455 claims whose audit verdict is unsupported, retained so that the audit is itself auditable; no chat item cites one. Self-containment. The release is self-contained. Nothing is linked and nothing requires an external resource to interpret. Sensitive and distressing content. The corpus contains disclosures about health, family, work and emotional distress, including material falling within the special categories of Article 9 of the GDPR. It contains that material necessarily: reply ignoring what someone has said about their health is not the correct reply. Readers and downstream users should expect content that is personal and at times distressing. Subpopulations. None can be identified. The persona layers demographic slots are empty on 147 of 160, so the corpus supports no analysis by demographic group and should not be used to attempt one. H.3 COLLECTION Source. The conversations come from the operational store of single mobile companion application, described in Appendix C.1. They were produced by people using deployed product for their own purposes, not by participants recruited to protocol, and every released turn is one the subject actually saw. Mechanism and timeframe. Records were exported from the production database. Observation windows run from each subjects first message to their last authored turn and span 36 to 120 days. H.4 PREPROCESSING AND LABELING Three passes were applied. Structural identifiers were removed and every turn was rewritten so that what was said survives and the words used to say it do not; dates were shifted by per-subject offset described in Appendix C.4. The rewriting cost 30 chat rows, withdrawn because the probe could not be released or its cited context was removed (Appendix D.5); its effect on retrieval and reply scores is not measured, since that would need the original wording, which is not released. Shadow replies and in-application game turns were removed. Labels were then derived by the five phases of Appendix D.1, and the result was graded by an independent audit and by the twenty-six mechanical gates released with the corpus. The original text is not released and is not recoverable from the release. The labeling and scoring software is distributed with the corpus. What the persona layer is not. The persona layer contains trait estimates and clinical-style summary, produced by language model from the conversation. Neither is validated psychological instrument. Neither was administered to the subject or reviewed by them, and the release terms permit no use of either as an assessment of any person. They are released because they are part of what the derivation produced, and because withholding derived layer while releasing the layer it came from would make the derivation uncheckable. H.5 USES The corpus has been used for the benchmark reported here and for nothing else. Appendix sets out uses outside machine learning that the record could support. What composition implies for future use. Ten subjects, one application, English text after surrogate substitution, and shifted dates. Rates may be computed only on the proportional stratum. Quantities conditioned on memory demand rest on five subjects under the strict reading and should not be reported as though they rested on ten.
