Any claim about whether these relationships benefited or harmed anyone: the corpus records that relationship continued, not what it did for the person in it. H.6 MAINTENANCE The corpus is maintained by the authors and reached at the contact address distributed with the release; both are withheld for anonymous review. Each release carries manifest naming every shipped file with its hash, so version is identified by content, and every repair applied since the first audit is recorded in statement distributed with it. Corrections will be issued as new versions under the same scheme, with prior manifests retained so that published result can be tied to the exact files it was computed on. The scoring package accepts submissions from others, and the procedure is documented with it.

sections.title: I DISCUSSION
sections.content: This paper uses the corpus for one thing: measuring whether system knows when to remember and what to remember. That is the narrowest use it has. What the release contains is ten people talking to the same companion for months, with what they said, what could be established about them, which turn established each claim, and how every label was reached. Several lines of work have wanted records of that kind and have not had them. This appendix sets out what each substituted instead, what recent work in each says the substitute costs, and which of their questions the record could answer: evaluation and conversational modeling (I.1), affect and mental state (I.2), the psychology of these relationships (I.3), and consumer research (I.4). Appendix I.5 states what the corpus cannot do. The pattern repeats in each case, and it is the pattern of Appendix B.1: field needed real people observed over time, could not obtain them, substituted something, and is now measuring what the substitution cost. I.1 MODELING PEOPLE IN CONVERSATION For this community, the corpus carries result about how people behave in conversation as well as dataset. Benchmarks decide in advance what person will need from reply. An authored question stands in for the moment person reaches back, and models judgment stands in for what the person meant (Appendix B.1). Proposition 2 prices the first substitution. benchmark that supplies context and measures the improvement reports the sum of two effects, one on messages that need the context and one on messages that do not, and it may credit the sum to the first only where the second is absent. On an authored corpus that holds by construction, because every question was written to need something. Real people rarely talk that way. Here the probes that need nothing earlier contribute twenty-four times as much of the measured gain as those that do. The result applies to any benchmark whose probes were written, and it rests on fact about people: most of what they say to companion concerns the present. The release also supports work scored benchmark does not. The restraint decision has per-probe supervision, 1,129 negatives against 404 positives, which is what training retrieval gate requires and what no other corpus supplies; the architectures surveyed in Appendix B.3 retrieve on every turn in part because nothing has ever told them when not to. The derivations are supervision of second kind, since each item records the referent resolver proposed, what verification kept of it, the rule that fixed the label and the turns the reply rested on, so model can be trained or evaluated on the intermediate decisions and not only on the outcome. And the coverage curve of Section 6 answers by measurement question the field answers by assertion: system holding the last thousand turns has everything it needs on 31% of memory-bearing probes, and reaching 95% takes ten thousand turns, which is longer than 9 of the 10 histories in this corpus. At these lengths, long context and retrieval are not alternatives.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: I.2 AFFECT, MENTAL STATE AND PREDICTION third line models the interaction itself, and it has moved in one direction over the past two years: from classifying turn to maintaining state that persists across turns. Zou et al. (2026) model the trajectory of affect through conversation, and Zhao et al. (2026b) argue for replacing stateless responder with one that carries psychological model of the person it is speaking to. Benchmarks have followed, with Iyer et al. (2026) scoring people and models on the same support dialogues. parallel effort attributes beliefs and intentions: Li et al. (2026a) ask whether conversational recommender infers what user wants, Wang et al. (2026) train responder on simulated user mental states directly, and Ni et al. (2026) survey the simulators on which most of this rests. closer line makes the internal state the object of evaluation. Yadav et al. (2026) ask model to infer beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions, knowledge and trust from dialogue, then to forecast how that dialogue continues from those inferences alone, and report that models identify the states and cannot use them to predict what follows. Bawatneh et al. (2026) score belief structures directly, over 895 narratives and some 22,000 labeled belief propositions, and find actor-specific belief tracking is where models fail. Zhao et al. (2026a) learn predictive representation of how affect unfolds and inject it into language model, evaluated across nine clip-level corpora. Cheng et al. (2026) run the argument the other way, fitting cognitive model of human decision-making to improve language models simulation of people in persuasion games, and Lin sets out what that practice can and cannot support. The dissociation Yadav et al. (2026) report is the one this paper finds on different axis: there model names mental state and cannot act on it, here model ranks probes needing memory above chance and cannot decide which to retrieve for. Each of these needs something it cannot observe. persistent psychological state is worth maintaining only if the person persists, and what these lines evaluate on does not persist: authored narratives, clip-length recordings, games that end, and support corpora that are largely single sessions between strangers, assembled for the purpose. mental-state attribution is worth scoring only against what someone actually wanted, and simulated user wants what it was told to want. The recurring move is to construct the state because it cannot be watched: the situated responder builds psychological world, the mental-state trainer simulates one. This corpus watches one instead. It records the same person across months, what they disclosed and when, what the companion said back, and whether they came back; its profile layer carries stressors, coping patterns and behaviors with the turns that established each and the window over which each held, so claim about someones state on day forty can be checked against what they said on day nine. It records that relationship continued. I.3 THE PSYCHOLOGY OF HUMANAI RELATIONSHIPS Outside machine learning, these relationships are studied directly, and Appendix B.5 describes what has been built: interview studies of how the bond develops over months, thematic analyses of the support people report receiving, and grounded-theory work on dependence and on distress when systems behavior changes. Pi & Hunter (2026) survey what longitudinal work exists, and Zhang et al. (2025b) report on well-being at scale. Every one of these studies is built from what people say about the interaction, through interviews, surveys, app reviews and forum posts. The interactions themselves are private, and this is the constraint that produced the three substitutions of Appendix B.1, met by different field and answered different way. What transcript adds is check. field whose evidence is self-report about an interaction has no way to compare the report against the interaction, and for ten people this corpus closes that gap. Some of what it shows is not what survey would return. The companion opens the exchange on 217 of the 430 participant-days, so the AI initiates these relationships about half the time. More than half of the companions messages offer tappable replies, and 33 of the 12,795 messages participants sent reproduce one, so the affordance the product invests in is almost entirely unused. Self-description fills where it asks for an interpretation and empties where it asks for category, 91.9% empty across demographic slots against 26.1% elsewhere, and it does so regardless of how much person said. And most of what people bring to companion concerns the present. Only 3.4% of their messages depend on anything said earlier, fact about companionship that work organized around memory would not predict. None of these is obtainable from an account of an interaction. All are obtainable from the interaction.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: I.4 CONSUMER RESEARCH AND MARKETING Consumer research has replaced its respondents. Synthetic panels, in which model is prompted into persona and asked what it would prefer or buy, are now routine in commercial practice, and the field has begun to audit them. Lukauskas & Šarkauskaite (2026) find such respondents plausible and not valid against psychometric criteria. Tigre & Souto (2026) propose diagnostics and corrections for consumer panels, which is itself statement that uncorrected panels are unreliable. Chen et al. (2026c) benchmark simulated survey responses across domains and report where they break. Maier et al. (2025) recover purchase intent under particular elicitation, which sharpens the question, since it shows the answer depends on how the model is asked. Beneath all of it sits the result of Venkit et al. (2026a): demographic attributes explain roughly 1.5% of the variance in how similarly two people respond, so persona assembled from them describes very nearly an unrelated person. Real self-description points the same way. In this corpus the demographic fields synthetic panel starts from are empty 156 times in 160, while the remaining persona fields are filled three times in four. Every one of these audits ends the same way, by asking for real responses to validate against, and preferably responses that were not produced for study. This corpus offers the field source of validation. synthetic persona can be held against real one whose every claim carries the turns that established it, confidence and the window over which it held. claim to reproduce individual difference can be held against people whose differences were recorded. The corpus is released for research and its terms permit nothing else. It may not be used to profile or target anyone, since the participants consented to research and to no other use, and the argument of this subsection is only that the question the field is publicly asking is the one the record answers. I.5 LIMITATIONS Ten people used one application over four months. They chose that product, so they are not sample of companion users and still less of people, and the application frames the relationship in particular way; how much of what is reported here survives different product is unknown. Every turn was rewritten during anonymization, so the corpus preserves what was said and not the words used to say it; the rewriting cost 30 chat rows (Appendix D.5), and its effect on retrieval and reply scores is not measured. Timestamps were shifted by per-subject offset, so intervals are exact while calendar position and day of the week carry no information. Three judgments rest on single reader. The on-screen verdicts of Appendix D.4 were made by one person over four passes, with the final rule reapplied to the earliest, and one reader means judgment without an agreement rate. The judge of Appendix A.2 agrees with that reader at κ = 0.804 on the binary use decision and 0.545 on the graded scale, so every graded score carries the weaker of the two. The question track carries content defect rate of 3.8% [3.2, 4.6] after repair, higher than the chat tracks, reported in Appendix D.8. Two results need their scope stated. Proposition 2 is about method and holds wherever the demand rate is below one; the 96% that instantiates it is about this corpus and this pair of conditions, and different pair would give different split. Under the strict reading, five subjects contribute no memory-bearing probes at all, so every quantity conditioned on memory demand is macro-average over five subjects with intervals to match, and none of them should be read as though it rested on ten.
